name: Duungidjawu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kite, Suzanne & Stephen Wurm. 2004. The Duungidjawu language of southeast Queensland: grammar, texts and vocabulary. Pacific Linguistics 553. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, Australian National University. Open access, ANU Open Research handle 1885/146174 (DOI 10.15144/PL-553).
catalog_locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 22; supporting sentence §2.2.1 Syllable structure, p. 20.
catalog_quote: In polysyllabic words with no long vowels, primary stress falls on the first syllable, and secondary stress falls on odd numbered syllables (e.g. yánjaràn 'old woman'). All long vowels bear stress. If the long vowel is in the first syllable of a word the stress pattern is as described above. If the long vowel is in the second syllable of a word, however, this syllable takes primary stress and the first syllable takes secondary stress (e.g. bìyá:yu 'two'). ... [§2.2.1, p. 20] The syllable structure in Duuŋidjawu is CV(C). There may be only one long vowel per word and this may occur in either the first or the second syllable (never in the third).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Kite, Suzanne & Stephen Wurm. 2004. The Duungidjawu language of southeast Queensland: grammar, texts and vocabulary. Pacific Linguistics 553. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (312 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'The Duungidjawu language of southeast Queensland: Grammar, texts and vocabulary', authors Kite & Wurm; cover note on p. 15: PL-553, DOI 10.15144/PL-553.1, online edition 2015 CC BY-SA 4.0). extracted text of p. 36 shows running head '22 Chapter 2' and heading '2.3 Stress'; the saved page render was viewed and the four sentences of the reported quote are there word for word, including the accented examples yánjaràn 'old woman' and bìyá:yu 'two' (the ANU text garbles these as 'yanjarim' and 'b'iya:yu'; the image is the authority). §2.3 is the entire stress section (five lines); the rest of the page is blank. Context read: §2.1.2 (p. 32-33)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on following odd-numbered syllables (a left-to-right trochaic pattern); vowel length overrides this: every long vowel is stressed, and a long vowel in the second syllable takes primary stress, demoting the initial syllable to secondary. So the language is initial-stress by default but sensitive to vowel length (weight).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables after the initial (yánjaràn); when a second-syllable long vowel takes primary stress the first syllable carries secondary stress (bìyá:yu).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the long-vowel cases are given as departures from the initial pattern; no lexical exceptions mentioned. Note that Holmer 1983 (Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland, Part I §2.9, p. 5, file), describing Wakka-Wakka proper and the wider Wakka group, states the opposite view: 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length' (Wakka-Wakka greeting wangá ngin janánde).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress (polysyllabic words), in the grammar's phonology chapter based on Wurm's 1955 fieldwork with Duungidjawu speakers; Holmer's second-syllable tendency is stated for 'words or utterances of some length', i.e. partly phrase-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Kite & Wurm 2004 describe Duungidjawu, which Glottolog 5.3 lists as a dialect (duun1241) of Wakawaka waka1274 (called 'a Waga dialect' in Kite's thesis title); the description rests on Wurm's 1955 fieldwork with the last speakers. Holmer 1983 describes Wakka-Wakka proper (the western Wakka group) from 1970s informants and reaches a different classification (stress not significant; tendency to second-syllable prominence in longer words). Cataloguers should record the statement as Duungidjawu and note Holmer's dissent for Wakka-Wakka.
